items.title: The Elizabethan Settlement (1559) was a deliberate compromise
items.claim: What did the Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559 establish?

options.text: Act of Supremacy (Elizabeth as 'Supreme Governor' — softer than 'Supreme Head'); Act of Uniformity (revised 1559 Prayer Book); Thirty-Nine Articles (1571 final) — a deliberately broad 'via media' between Catholic and Reformed

items.reveal:
Elizabeth's first Parliament (1559) produced the legislation by narrow margins — particularly the Act of Supremacy, opposed by all 18 surviving bishops from Mary's reign. The 1559 Prayer Book combined elements of Cranmer's 1549 and 1552 books, with deliberately ambiguous language on the Eucharist.

The Act of Uniformity required attendance at parish church on pain of fines. The Thirty-Nine Articles (1563, finalised 1571) defined Anglican doctrine. The Settlement was challenged by Puritans wanting further reform and by Catholic recusants.

Elizabeth reportedly said she would not 'open windows into men's souls' — outward conformity was required; private belief was largely left alone.
items.why: The Church of England's modern shape — episcopal, vernacular, broad — is a 1559 political compromise that became national habit over 45 years. One of the most successful exercises in deliberate ambiguity in European history.

items.title: The US Vietnam draft was decided by a televised lottery
items.claim: How was the Vietnam draft (Selective Service) administered after 1969?

options.text: Strict order by date of birth, alphabetical
On 1 December 1969, blue capsules with birthdates were drawn from a glass jar on national TV — men born on dates drawn first were called up first
By state quota with each state choosing its own method

items.reveal:
The 1 December 1969 lottery selected 19-26 year olds. 366 capsules (one per birthday including 29 February) were drawn live. Men with low numbers (1-195) were called; high numbers (typically 196+) were spared.

The statistical method was later shown to have biased the draw — capsules added in order from January were less thoroughly mixed, so December birthdays were over-represented at low numbers.

Deferments before 1969 — for university students, for medical reasons — disproportionately spared the wealthy. Around 2.7 million Americans served in Vietnam; 58,220 died. The draft ended in 1973.
items.why: Even apparently neutral mechanisms encode injustice. The Vietnam draft's class bias before 1969, and the statistical bias of the 1969 lottery itself, are case studies in how 'fairness' breaks down in practice.

items.title: Mary I burned around 280 Protestants
items.claim: Mary I's reign (1553-1558) earned the 'Bloody Mary' epithet through executions. How many died?

options.text: Around 10,000 — comparable to Henry VIII's executions
Around 280 Protestants burned at the stake, plus 30 who died in prison — a smaller toll than Henry VIII's or Elizabeth I's overall execution numbers
Over 50,000 in a state campaign of terror
No confirmed executions for religion — the epithet is entirely myth

items.reveal:
John Foxe's 'Actes and Monuments' (1563, later 'Foxe's Book of Martyrs') chronicled the Marian burnings in vivid detail and became a foundational Protestant text. Henry VIII executed an estimated 57,000 (Holinshed's figure, contested) including thousands of vagrants; Elizabeth I executed around 200 Catholic priests and Jesuits.

Mary's numbers were lower in absolute terms but concentrated (1555-1558) and ideological. The propaganda effect outlasted the regime.
items.why: Reputation is unevenly distributed. Mary's image as uniquely cruel says more about the durability of Protestant propaganda than about Tudor execution rates.
